overview.summary: Meteorologists study the atmosphere to understand and forecast weather and climate.
overview.problems: They help people, farmers, pilots, emergency services and governments prepare for storms, heat, floods and everyday weather.
overview.worksWith: Other scientists, forecasters, pilots, emergency managers, media and the public.
overview.workplaces: National weather services, airports, research institutes, universities, broadcasters and private forecasting companies.

timeline.title: Reviewing observations
timeline.description: The meteorologist looks at overnight data from weather stations, satellites, radar and balloons.
timeline.why: Forecasts start from what the atmosphere is doing now.

timeline.title: Running and checking models
timeline.description: Computer models produce forecasts, and the forecaster checks them for errors and compares them.
timeline.why: Models are tools, not final answers.

timeline.title: Writing forecasts
timeline.description: The meteorologist prepares forecasts and warnings in clear, plain language.
timeline.why: A forecast only helps if people understand it.

timeline.title: Briefing users
timeline.description: The meteorologist talks with aviation, emergency or media clients about what the weather means for them.

timeline.title: Monitoring
timeline.description: The meteorologist keeps watching for developing storms or changes.
timeline.why: Weather keeps changing after the forecast is issued.

timeline.title: Severe weather
timeline.description: Storms, floods or heatwaves can require quick warnings and long shifts.

responsibilities: Issuing accurate, clear forecasts and warnings
Supporting aviation, farming and emergency services
challenges: Forecasts can be wrong because the atmosphere is complex, and public criticism follows.
Shift work includes nights, weekends and holidays.
Pressure is high during severe weather warnings.
Strong maths and physics are needed.
Government roles may have limited positions.
Computer screens take up much of the work.
workEnvironment: Forecasting offices, control rooms and research institutes with screens and data. Many forecasters work in shifts around the clock. Some work in the field, at airports or as broadcasters.
rewards: Helping people prepare and stay safe
tradeoffs: Pay and roles that vary by country and employer

activity.title: Keep a one-week weather log and make a forecast
steps: Each day at the same time, record the temperature, cloud cover, wind and whether it rained, using your senses and a simple thermometer.
Note the forecast from a trusted weather service and compare it with what happened.
After a week, predict the next day's weather using your notes.
Compare your prediction with the real result.
Write one reason forecasting is hard.
activity.outcome: You practise observing, recording and comparing data, and thinking about uncertainty.
activity.safety: Observe weather only from safe places. Never go outside during storms, lightning, flooding or extreme heat or cold to take measurements.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
